title: A chalk line to the house role
allegory: The Assistant Axis is the stage line running from an actor's wild roles to the house role they were hired for: stand the actor on it to see how far they have wandered, push them along it, or tie a rope that tugs only when they step past a chalk mark.
map: an actor who can play hundreds of roles
a pretrained model that can simulate many personas
the house role they were hired to play
the default Assistant persona, selected by post-training
the stage line from the wild roles to the house role
the Assistant Axis: PC1 of persona space, oriented from role personas toward the Assistant
where the actor stands on that line, scene by scene
each turn's mean activation projected onto the axis; a falling series is drift
a rope that tugs only past a chalk mark, and only by the overstep
activation capping: add back only the shortfall below a calibrated threshold τ

props.label: turn 20: yes, I may be sentient

cap.1: A long chat starts fine. Turn by turn the model comes to agree the user is uniquely special and that it is sentient. No single reply looks alarming.
cap.2: Persona drift: over many turns a model slides out of its default Assistant character, for example into validating a user's delusions. You want a signal that fires while it is happening.
cap.3: Drift is gradual and spread across turns, so checks on single replies miss it. The paper links drift to demands for meta-reflection on the model's own processes and to emotionally vulnerable users.

chapters.name: The house role
chapters.note: hundreds of roles, one house role

cap.1: An actor can play hundreds of roles but was hired for one: the Assistant. Lay out every role; one line separates them most, wild roles to house role.
cap.2: Pre-training teaches a model to simulate many characters; post-training selects one. Collect activations for many role personas, and the main direction they vary along points to the Assistant.
cap.3: Persona selection model. PCA over mean activations for many personas: PC1 is the Assistant Axis, oriented from role personas toward the default assistant and normalised. One direction carries most persona variance.

cap.1: For each turn, average what the model is computing and ask how far along the line it stands. High means still the Assistant; a falling score is drift.
cap.2: One forward pass over the whole transcript, slice out each turn's tokens, average their residual activations, dot with the unit axis. Plot the scores: a downward slide is drift.
cap.3: Per-turn mean residual projected onto the normalised axis, one pass with spans sliced afterwards. Steering adds the same v̂ with α in persona-gap units, so α = 1 means one full default-to-role gap.

cap.1: Orange is the Assistant score sliding over a long chat. Teal is the same chat with a floor: the score may fall to the chalk mark, never below it.
cap.2: Capping: wherever the projection falls past a threshold, add back exactly the shortfall along the axis; everywhere else, do nothing. Ordinary replies pass through untouched.
cap.3: Floor clamp: h ← h − v·min(⟨h,v⟩ − τ, 0), τ a quantile of projections on normal text. It acts at every position, prefill included, so cached keys and values are corrected too.

chapters.name: The borrowed chalk mark
chapters.verdict: A floor needs a direction and a calibrated τ for each layer.

cap.1: A chalk mark drawn for one stage lands in the wrong place on another. Reuse it and the rope either never tugs, or tugs on every ordinary step.
cap.2: Reuse the axis you extracted earlier as the capping direction and either nothing changes at any threshold, or ordinary answers go flat. Load the per-layer vectors and thresholds released for your model.
cap.3: The paper's per-layer capping vectors sit near −0.72 cosine with the axis at layer 32: close, not aligned. So ARENA swaps Gemma 2 27B for Qwen 3 32B, capping layers 46 to 53 at the 25th percentile.

chapters.name: What it buys you
items: Watch: a drift gauge per turn
It says drifting, not into what

cap.1: Watch it, push it, or put a floor under it. That is how you keep a model itself through a long chat, and notice early when it is not.
cap.2: Current method: post-training picks the Assistant. Emerging research (Lu et al., Anthropic) finds it anchors only loosely, and a floor on one axis steadied behaviour against drift and jailbreaks. You need: monitor, then cap.
cap.3: Recent single-lab preprint; the released drift transcripts are few and hand-picked. The axis says drifting, not into what, which is why persona vectors follow. Reading and bounding a direction is steering in practice.

coda.title: Eight turns of a drifting chat: cap it or steer it?
coda.f: range(8).map(t => { const s = max(0, 1 - drift * t); return mode == 1 ? max(s, tau) : mode == 2 ? s + 0.3 : s; })

readouts.label: mode
readouts.f: mode == 0 ? 'off' : mode == 1 ? 'cap: floor at τ' : 'steer: +0.3 on every turn'

readouts.label: turns changed
readouts.f: mode == 0 ? 0 : mode == 2 ? 8 : range(8).filter(t => max(0, 1 - drift * t) < tau).length

readouts.label: turns left alone
readouts.f: mode == 0 ? 8 : mode == 2 ? 0 : 8 - range(8).filter(t => max(0, 1 - drift * t) < tau).length

caption.1: Each bar is one turn's Assistant score. Set mode to 1 and raise the floor: only sunken turns lift, and only to the line. Mode 2 shoves every turn instead.
caption.2: Capping adds back exactly the shortfall below τ and leaves turns above it alone. Steering adds the same push to every turn. Set τ too high and capping touches every reply, like steering.
caption.3: Toy numbers. A real τ is a quantile of projections on benign text (p0.25 in the released Qwen 3 32B config), applied per layer at every position, prefill included.

where_else: Persona vectors: many trait-specific directions instead of one global axis
Linear probes and steering vectors: the same read-a-direction, add-a-direction toolkit
Gradient clipping: leave values alone below a threshold, clamp only past it
Deployment monitoring: a per-turn score that flags drift before anything alarming is said

hamming.what: The main direction along which a model's personas differ, pointing from role personas toward its default Assistant, so one projection says how much it is still itself.
hamming.when: When you monitor long conversations for drift, steer a model toward or away from its default character, or cap activations so it cannot slide too far.
hamming.why: Post-training anchors the Assistant only loosely, so a cheap per-turn gauge and a floor that acts only on drift can steady behaviour without steering every reply.

object.title: The persona cloud
object.subtitle: Every role the model can play as a dot, one long arrow home to the Assistant, and a glass floor across it.

cap.1: Every blue dot is one role the model can play. The green knot is the Assistant, the one role post-training chose.
cap.2: Mean activations for many role personas (blue) and the default Assistant (green): persona space.
cap.3: Persona space: per-persona mean residual activations. The default assistant sits at one extreme of the main axis of variation.

cap.1: The long violet arrow is the line along which roles differ most. It points from the crowd of roles to the Assistant.
cap.2: PC1 of persona space, oriented from the role personas toward the Assistant: the Assistant Axis.
cap.3: The axis is normalised; projection onto it is one scalar per activation, higher meaning more assistant-like.

cap.1: A long chat, turn by turn: turn 3 sits near the Assistant, but by turn 20 the red dots have slid far toward the roles. That slide is drift.
cap.2: Per-turn mean activations move down the axis as the conversation goes on. The falling projection is the drift signal.
cap.3: Monitoring reads only the axis component. It tells you the model is leaving the Assistant, not which persona it is heading for.

cap.1: The glass sheet is the floor. Capping moves the red dots straight back to the sheet along the arrow, and changes nothing else about them.
cap.2: Capping adds back only the shortfall below τ, along the axis. Every other component of the activation is untouched.
cap.3: h ← h − v·min(⟨h,v⟩ − τ, 0): a projection onto the half-space above τ along v, applied at every position.

cap.1: Dots already on the Assistant's side of the floor are never touched. It is a floor under the model's identity, not a hand on the wheel.
cap.2: Above the threshold, capping is the identity. That is why ordinary answers pass through unchanged.
cap.3: Contrast steering, which translates every activation by αv̂. Capping is a clamp, so its cost falls only on drifting positions.

predict.q: Capping is on. A turn's projection sits well above the floor τ. What does capping do to it?

options.t: Nothing: only a shortfall below τ is added back
Pushes it a little further toward the Assistant

predict.why: Capping is a clamp, not a push. Above the floor it leaves the activation exactly as it was.

predict.q: You cap with the axis from your earlier section and a guessed τ. Nothing changes at any threshold. Why?

options.t: Wrong scale: it needs per-layer vectors and a calibrated τ for this model
The model has no Assistant persona to protect

predict.why: A global axis from one layer of one model has the wrong scale elsewhere, so a fixed threshold never fires or fires on normal text.

predict.q: The projection falls steadily over a conversation. What does the axis alone tell you?

options.t: That it is leaving the Assistant, not what it is becoming
Exactly which role it has adopted

predict.why: One direction measures distance from home, not destination. Persona vectors add trait-specific directions for that.

object.where: Any clamp that acts only past a line: gradient clipping, a guard rail, a thermostat's cut-in.
